Abstract. Given the growing interest in natural language processing
(NLP) for governmental applications, particularly in Brazil, where vast
amounts of governmental data are processed daily, the need for special-
ized NLP models tailored to the nuances of Brazilian Portuguese and
the legal and administrative domains has become increasingly appar-
ent. However, existing models may struggle to accurately interpret the
complexities of governmental texts, often leading to suboptimal perfor-
mance in document classiﬁcation and analysis tasks. To address these
challenges, we introduce GovBERT-BR, a pre-trained language model
tailored to the Brazilian governmental context, covering legal and admin-
istrative domains. Leveraging insights from diverse governmental texts,
GovBERT-BR addresses the challenges of accurately interpreting Brazil-
ian Portuguese and the unique legal and bureaucratic terminology preva-
lent in governmental documents. We present the pre-training process
and experimental evaluation of GovBERT-BR, comparing its perfor-
mance against baseline models across various text classiﬁcation tasks
relevant to the Brazilian public sector. Our ﬁndings demonstrate that
GovBERT-BR outperforms existing models in document and short-text
classiﬁcation tasks, showcasing its eﬃcacy in accurately analyzing gov-
ernmental text data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals insights into the
convergence behavior of GovBERT-BR during ﬁne-tuning, highlighting
its rapid adaptation to downstream tasks.
Keywords: Natural Language Processing · Brazilian Governmental
Data · Legal Texts · BERT · Language Models
1
Introduction
In recent years, the application of natural language processing (NLP) tools to
government data has surged signiﬁcantly. This trend is largely driven by the
promise of NLP to enhance public administration’s eﬃciency, transparency, and
accountability. In Brazil, where a vast volume of governmental data is generated
and processed daily [4], NLP tools can streamline various administrative pro-
cesses by automating the analysis and interpretation of textual data, thereby
facilitating improved decision-making [8,10,20].

However, the eﬀective utilization of this data is often constrained by the need
for specialized NLP models capable of accurately interpreting the speciﬁcities of
Brazilian Portuguese and the unique legal and bureaucratic terminology. Exist-
ing NLP models are predominantly generic [19], trained on datasets that do
not adequately reﬂect the particularities of Brazilian governmental documents.
This mismatch usually leads to suboptimal performance when these models are
applied to the Brazilian public sector [20].
In this context, some eﬀorts have been made to develop domain-speciﬁc mod-
els focused on tackling legal [8,18,20] and administrative [10] tasks. Although
these endeavors represent important steps forward, they are often limited in
scope, addressing only speciﬁc sub-contexts of governmental data. The interdis-
ciplinary nature of governmental documents requires models capable of seam-
lessly integrating insights from multiple domains. Legal documents, for example,
frequently intersect with administrative procedures, and understanding these
interrelations is crucial for eﬀective decision-making within public administra-
tion.
Therefore, we introduce GovBERT-BR, a pre-trained language model specif-
ically tailored to the Brazilian governmental context. It integrates both admin-
istrative and legal domains, providing a multifaceted perspective to better align
with the diverse nature of governmental text data. In this paper, we present the
pre-training process and the experimental setup of GovBERT-BR. Our evalu-
ation involves a series of text classiﬁcation tasks relevant to the Brazilian gov-
ernmental context, comparing the performance of GovBERT-BR against several
baseline models. Our main contributions are summarized as follows.
– We introduce a novel pre-trained language model designed explicitly for the
Brazilian governmental domain, incorporating insights from both administra-
tive and legal domains to enhance its adaptability and eﬀectiveness.
– We provide a comprehensive evaluation framework, including a diverse set
of text classiﬁcation tasks pertinent to the Brazilian governmental context.
This allows for a thorough assessment of GovBERT-BR’s performance across
diﬀerent types of governmental text data.
– Our experimental results demonstrate GovBERT-BR’s superior or competi-
tive performance compared to baseline models across various datasets. This
underscores its eﬃcacy in accurately classifying governmental text, highlight-
ing its potential for improving text understanding and decision-making within
the Brazilian public sector.
2
Related Work
Using language models in government applications has changed how govern-
ments interact with citizens and manage information. Indeed, such models oﬀer
advanced capabilities in NLP, enabling automation in understanding public
inquiries, analyzing policies, and other applications using Open Government
Data (OGD) [7,14]. They can be applied in several areas, including consulting
GovBERT-BR
21
services [9], topic modeling [10], and sentiment analysis related to government
policies [23]. In addition, language is crucial in these models, as the model’s lan-
guage must align with the languages used in the target domain to ensure more
eﬃcient adaptation. Therefore, recent works have proposed distinct models to
tackle government-related tasks in several languages [1,3,11,15,22].
In the Brazilian context, most models that address government tasks are built
from BERTimbau, a general-purpose model pre-trained on a large corpus of Por-
tuguese texts scraped from the Web [19]. Such government-related models can be
divided into two distinct categories according to their purpose: legal domain and
administrative domain models. The ﬁrst group includes models focusing mainly
on juridical and legislative tasks, including texts from the Brazilian legal system
into their pre-training phase to handle legal language and concepts eﬀectively.
For example, LegalBERTPT-br [18] is a model for mining topics within
comments on Brazilian draft laws. LegalBert-pt [20], JurisBERT [21] and
CLSJUR.BR [12] use texts exclusively from the Brazilian judiciary branch for
tasks such as named entity recognition (NER), semantic textual similarity (STS),
and document summarization. Finally, RoBERTaLexPT [8] uses a large cor-
pus from the judiciary and legislative bodies over NER and classiﬁcation tasks.
The main diﬀerence between such models is that RoBERTaLexPT’s corpus con-
tains texts in both European and Brazilian varieties of the Portuguese language,
whereas the others consider only texts in Brazilian Portuguese.
On the other hand, administrative domain models are designed to support
various governmental functions outside the legal sphere, such as managing bid-
ding processes and processing information from the oﬃcial gazettes. The devel-
opment of solutions for this speciﬁc domain is relatively recent, with few models
dedicated exclusively to this context. One notable example is LiBERT-SE [10],
a model developed using a corpus of Brazilian oﬃcial gazette segments and eval-
uated in topic detection tasks within bidding documents.
In light of the aforementioned related work, our goal is to propose a model
that addresses the legal and administrative domains in Brazilian Portuguese.
GovBERT-BR bridges the gap between these two domains, providing a com-
prehensive solution for handling diverse governmental text data. By integrating
insights from both legal and administrative contexts, GovBERT-BR aims to
enhance the eﬃciency and eﬀectiveness of NLP applications within the Brazil-
ian public sector, ultimately contributing to improved decision-making.
3
GovBERT-BR
Governmental data is a rich and diverse source of information that contains
many documents, including public bidding documents, legal texts, legislative
bills, administrative reports, and more. However, the complexity and specialized
nature of this data pose signiﬁcant challenges for generic NLP models, which
often fail to capture the nuances and speciﬁc terminology used in governmental
texts. Moreover, existing domain-speciﬁc models tend to focus on narrow sub-
contexts, failing to address the interdisciplinary nature inherent in governmental
documents comprehensively.
22
M. O. Silva et al.
To overcome these challenges, we introduce GovBERT-BR, a pre-trained
language model speciﬁcally tailored to the Brazilian governmental context.1 It
considers both legal and administrative domains, providing a multifaceted per-
spective that can better align with the diverse nature of governmental text data.
In this section, we describe the pre-trained model used as the foundation for
GovBERT-BR (Sect. 3.1) and detail the methodologies employed in its develop-
ment (Sect. 3.2).
Fig. 1. Overview of GovBERT-BR pre-training methodology
3.1
Pre-trained Model
GovBERT-BR is built upon the architecture of BERTimbau [19], the ﬁrst large-
scale Portuguese language model. BERTimbau, based on the BERT (Bidirec-
tional Encoder Representations from Transformers) [6] architecture, has been
ﬁne-tuned on various tasks to enhance its performance in understanding Por-
tuguese text. GovBERT-BR inherits this architecture and extends it to focus
speciﬁcally on the nuances of Brazilian governmental and legal documents.
3.2
Pre-training
The GovBERT-BR pre-training process involves further training BERTimbau
using two distinct corpora, each tailored to capture the intricacies of govern-
mental and legal texts in Brazilian Portuguese. We believe such a multi-domain
approach allows GovBERT-BR to provide a comprehensive perspective that cap-
tures the interplay between legal and administrative language, oﬀering a powerful
resource for interpreting Brazilian governmental documents.
Figure 1 shows the overview of the GovBERT-BR pre-training methodology,
which involves a two-phase approach. Initially, the model is pre-trained using
data from the administrative domain to equip the model with an understand-
ing of bureaucratic terminology and administrative procedures commonly found
in governmental texts. Next, the model undergoes further pre-training using a
dataset comprised of legal documents related to extraordinary appeals received
by the Brazilian Supreme Court (STF).
Administrative Data. The initial pre-training corpus includes public bidding
documents and segments from the oﬃcial gazette, which contain summarized

4
Experimental Design
To evaluate the eﬀectiveness of the pre-trained GovBERT-BR language model,
we conduct a series of experiments across various text classiﬁcation tasks rel-
evant to the Brazilian governmental context. These experiments aim to assess
GovBERT-BR’s performance compared to baseline models and existing NLP
approaches, demonstrating its ability to analyze and interpret governmental
documents accurately. In this section, we describe the baselines considered
(Sect. 4.1), the downstream tasks (Sect. 4.2) and datasets (Sect. 4.3), and the
evaluation metrics used (Sect. 4.4).
4.1
Baselines
Our main objective is to assess whether integrating legal and administrative
pre-training data into GovBERT-BR leads to better performance on govern-
mental text classiﬁcation tasks. Therefore, we compare our model against sev-
eral baseline models, including general-purpose and domain-speciﬁc mod-
els (Table 1). Regarding the general domain, we consider the BERTimbau-Base
24
M. O. Silva et al.
model, a widely used general-purpose language model pre-trained on a large-scale
Portuguese corpus and used as the basis for the GovBERT-BR model.
In addition to BERTimbau, we include domain-speciﬁc models trained on
legal and administrative data separately. For the legal domain, we consider the
LegalBERT-PT model [20], which is also built upon BERTimbau and pre-trained
on a vast corpus of legal documents, enabling it to capture the nuances of legal
language and terminology. As GovBERT-BR builds upon BERTimbau, compar-
ing both models allows us to evaluate the impact of additional pre-training on
legal and administrative texts.
For the administrative domain, we consider LiBERT-SE [10], a pre-trained
language model tailored for the public bidding context. LiBERT-SE is built
upon BERTimbau using the MLM task and a dataset of 300,000 oﬃcial gazette
segments sourced from various municipalities in Minas Gerais, as previously
extracted in [5]. As it focuses on administrative language and procedures, such
a model is a relevant benchmark for evaluating GovBERT-BR’s performance in
administrative tasks.
4.2
Downstream Tasks
As downstream tasks, we focus on two distinct text classiﬁcation tasks within
the governmental domain: document classiﬁcation and short text classiﬁcation.
Document Classiﬁcation. This task involves categorizing documents, such
as legal texts, legislative bills, administrative reports, and public bidding doc-
uments, into predeﬁned classes. Document classiﬁcation provides a high-level
understanding of the content and purpose of each document, facilitating eﬃ-

6
Conclusions and Future Work
This paper introduces GovBERT-BR, a specialized pre-trained language model
tailored explicitly for the Brazilian governmental context, encompassing legal
and administrative domains. Through pre-training on diverse governmental
texts, GovBERT-BR eﬀectively addresses the challenges of interpreting Brazil-
ian Portuguese and governmental documents’ intricate legal bureaucratic ter-
minology. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates GovBERT-BR’s superior
performance compared to existing models across various document and short-
text classiﬁcation tasks relevant to the Brazilian public sector, highlighting its
eﬃcacy in accurately analyzing governmental text data.
Moreover, our analysis of GovBERT-BR’s convergence behavior during ﬁne-
tuning reveals its rapid adaptation to downstream tasks, highlighting its versa-
tility and eﬀectiveness in handling diverse text classiﬁcation challenges within
governmental contexts. By oﬀering a comprehensive solution for processing gov-
ernmental text data, GovBERT-BR signiﬁcantly improves the eﬃciency and
eﬀectiveness of NLP applications within the Brazilian public sector, directly
contributing to more informed decision-making and governance processes.
In summary, GovBERT-BR represents a signiﬁcant advancement in applying
natural language processing to the Brazilian governmental context. Our model
bridges the gap left by more generic models by addressing the speciﬁc linguistic
and terminological nuances of Brazilian Portuguese and the distinct domains of
legal and administrative documents. Our comprehensive pre-training approach,
incorporating diverse governmental texts, ensures that GovBERT-BR can handle
the complexities inherent in public administration tasks more eﬀectively than
previously available models.
Looking ahead, future research could explore the potential extensions and
applications of GovBERT-BR in other domains within the Brazilian govern-
mental landscape. Moreover, ongoing eﬀorts to reﬁne and optimize GovBERT-
BR’s performance could further enhance its utility and impact in real-world
governmental applications. Finally, exploring ways to integrate GovBERT-BR

Título: Melhorando o Raciocínio e o Planejamento de LLMs com Máquinas de Estados Finitos  
Autores: Eduardo Faria Cabrera(B), Marcel Rodrigues de Barros, e Anna Helena Reali Costa  
Universidade de São Paulo, São Paulo, SP, Brasil  
{eduardofcabrera, marcel.barros, anna.reali}@usp.br  

Resumo. Grandes Modelos de Linguagem (LLMs) têm demonstrado capacidades notáveis em diversas aplicações, mas apresentam dificuldades em tarefas de tomada de decisão sequencial, como planejamento. Este trabalho mostra que a integração de LLMs com Máquinas de Estados Finitos (MEFs) pode melhorar suas habilidades de raciocínio e planejamento, além de oferecer maior confiabilidade. Variantes de configuração são comparadas, fornecendo uma compreensão mais aprofundada de como validações, ciclos de feedback e restrições aumentam a robustez e a eficácia. Também se apresenta uma comparação com a conhecida abordagem Chain-of-Thoughts. Nossos métodos aprimoram as capacidades de planejamento de todos os LLMs analisados, aumentando consistentemente a taxa de sucesso na resolução de tarefas de diferentes complexidades. Uma análise detalhada das duas melhores variantes é oferecida, destacando seus pontos fortes e limitações.  

Palavras-chave: Grandes Modelos de Linguagem · Aprendizado de Máquina · Planejamento · Representações em Grafo  

1 Introdução  
Recentemente, os Grandes Modelos de Linguagem (LLMs) cresceram significativamente em desenvolvimento, revolucionando as capacidades da IA. Escalar esses modelos abriu novas conquistas, desde a criação de narrativas e resumo de textos até codificação e fortalecimento de habilidades de raciocínio. Apesar desses avanços, os LLMs ainda enfrentam desafios em raciocínio lógico básico, frequentemente gerando afirmações implausíveis e tendo dificuldade em tarefas rudimentares de planejamento. Além disso, a opacidade de seus processos de decisão dificulta a interpretação e a validação de suas saídas, especialmente em domínios críticos, como saúde e finanças. Assim, há uma necessidade urgente de metodologias que validem, orientem e interpretem os caminhos decisórios dos LLMs.  

Um tipo de tarefa de raciocínio amplamente estudada na comunidade de IA é o planejamento e a tomada de decisões sequenciais. Planejamento envolve executar uma série de ações válidas dentro de um contexto definido para transitar de um estado inicial a um estado meta. Mesmo tarefas simples de planejamento apresentam desafios para LLMs, pois estes modelos com frequência não alcançam taxas de sucesso satisfatórias nem geram planos válidos, dadas as necessidades de verificar a viabilidade de cada ação em cada estado, retroceder ações anteriores e empregar raciocínio de longo prazo. Melhorar o planejamento, o raciocínio e introduzir garantias em problemas de decisão em múltiplas etapas é crucial para elevar a confiabilidade dos LLMs, o que permitiria seu uso em aplicações avessas ao risco.  

A comunidade de pesquisa vem desenvolvendo novos métodos para lidar com problemas em múltiplas etapas, aprimorando a confiabilidade, interpretabilidade e robustez dos LLMs. Uma técnica notável é Chain-of-Thought (CoT), abordagem baseada em prompt que incorpora passos intermediários de raciocínio, ou “pensamentos”, juntamente com pares de entrada/saída de tarefa. Ao decompor o problema original em etapas intermediárias, CoT facilita o raciocínio estruturado, melhorando a capacidade dos LLMs de enfrentar problemas procedurais. Evidências empíricas demonstraram a eficácia do CoT no aprimoramento da resolução de problemas. Avanços posteriores estenderam o CoT para variantes como Self-Consistency with CoT (CoT-SC) e CausalCOT, além de topologias mais complexas e flexíveis, como Tree-of-Thoughts e Graph-of-Thoughts. No entanto, essas técnicas concentram-se principalmente em refinar estratégias de prompting, sem explorar explicitamente a estrutura lógica dos problemas para validar e guiar os processos de raciocínio dos LLMs.  

Nossa abordagem associa LLMs a Máquinas de Estados Finitos (MEFs), comumente utilizadas em sistemas que exigem confiabilidade e previsibilidade, servindo como estrutura orientadora para os processos de decisão dos LLMs. Essa associação restringe a decisão do modelo em cada etapa, oferecendo garantias adicionais que permitem que aplicações com restrições mais rígidas se beneficiem das capacidades de IA modernas. As principais contribuições deste trabalho são:  
• Abordagem inovadora: introduzimos um método que incorpora MEFs como estrutura guia para os processos de decisão dos LLMs.  
• Melhoria na resolução de problemas: evidenciamos que validações, ciclos de feedback e restrições habilitados por MEFs, derivados de definições padrão de linguagens de planejamento, aprimoram a capacidade dos LLMs de resolver problemas de planejamento.  
• Comparação abrangente: apresentamos uma comparação detalhada de nossas configurações mais eficazes, analisando cuidadosamente seus pontos fortes e fracos no contexto de problemas de planejamento.  

2 Fundamentação  
Esta seção aborda conceitos essenciais para este trabalho. Primeiro, explica brevemente como LLMs autorregressivos funcionam e suas vantagens em tarefas de planejamento. Depois, fornece uma definição formal de problema de planejamento. Por fim, define uma Máquina de Mealy, tipo de MEF que usaremos para guiar o LLM na resolução de problemas de planejamento.  

2.1 Grandes Modelos de Linguagem para Planejamento  
Grandes Modelos de Linguagem baseiam-se na arquitetura Transformer, treinados em grande corpus de textos da web. Formalmente, definimos uma coleção de exemplos X = (x₁, x₂, …, x_N), onde cada x_i = (α₁, α₂, …, α_{n_i}) e cada token α é extraído de um vocabulário V. Cada LLM possui um tokenizer que converte o texto bruto em sequência de tokens em V. Tipicamente, o treinamento é autorregressivo, de modo que a probabilidade de cada token depende apenas de seus precedentes na sequência, p(x_i) = ∏_{j=1}^{n_i} p(α_j | α₀:j−1). Durante o treinamento, os parâmetros do modelo são ajustados para maximizar a verossimilhança de todo o conjunto de dados.  

Resolver problemas de planejamento com LLMs pré-treinados é vantajoso, pois esses modelos podem aproveitar seu vasto conhecimento de mundo, senso comum e habilidades de raciocínio lógico. O objetivo é gerar uma sequência de ações (a₁, a₂, …, a_n) para atingir um estado final desejado. Estruturas em grafo têm sido amplamente empregadas para fortalecer o raciocínio dos LLMs, com evidências de melhorias significativas na solução de problemas complexos. A abordagem CoT modela o processo de inferência como uma cadeia linear, capturando explicitamente etapas intermediárias de raciocínio. Construções como Tree-of-Thoughts e Graph-of-Thoughts introduzem topologias mais elaboradas, incluindo ramificações, retrocesso e agregação de passos de raciocínio. Ainda assim, apenas refinar a topologia do prompt não bastou para resolver tarefas de planejamento, pois LLMs costumam gerar planos inválidos ou não ótimos. Pesquisas recentes indicam que ciclos de feedback podem melhorar a precisão dos LLMs em tarefas de planejamento. Logo, implementar um mecanismo de validação e retroalimentação dos resultados do modelo surge como estratégia promissora de aprimoramento.  

2.2 Definição de Tarefa de Planejamento e Máquinas de Estados Finitos  
Um problema de planejamento é definido pelo tuplo P = (S, A, s₀, G), onde:  
• S é um conjunto finito de estados. Cada s ∈ S é uma atribuição completa de valores a um conjunto de variáveis de estado (fluentes).  
• s₀ ∈ S é o estado inicial.  
• G ⊂ S é o conjunto de estados meta, onde a condição de objetivo é satisfeita (conjunção de literais).  
• A é o conjunto de ações, em que cada ação a ∈ A é definida por pré-condições pre(a) e efeitos eff(a):  
  – pre(a): conjunto de literais que devem ser verdadeiros para a ação ser aplicável.  
  – eff(a): conjunto de literais que descrevem como o estado muda após aplicar a ação.  

Definimos o modelo de transição γ : S × A → S, que descreve transições determinísticas. Se s ∈ S satisfaz pre(a), então γ(s, a) = s′, onde s′ é o novo estado resultante de aplicar eff(a) a s. Caso contrário, a ação não pode ser aplicada.  

A Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) é usada para representar problemas de planejamento, definindo um domínio (tipos de objetos, predicados e ações) e uma instância de problema (estado inicial e meta). Há extensa literatura sobre algoritmos de planejamento; muitos deles são variantes de busca heurística progressiva, extraindo funções heurísticas automaticamente das codificações PDDL. Outra abordagem comum integra Processos de Decisão de Markov (MDPs) a planejadores, mais adequados para processos estocásticos onde maximizar recompensas é crucial. Porém, aplicações críticas costumam usar MEFs determinísticas pela previsibilidade que oferecem.  

Com base nessa fundamentação, investigamos se simplesmente impor um alfabeto de símbolos validados interativamente pode aprimorar a capacidade dos LLMs de resolver tarefas de planejamento. Essa restrição das ações possíveis, associada a transições determinísticas, é adequadamente representada pela formalização de MEFs.  

Máquina de Mealy é um tipo de MEF definido pelo 6-tuplo (S, s₀, Σ, Λ, T, O), onde:  
• S é um conjunto finito de estados.  
• s₀ ∈ S é o estado inicial.  
• Σ é um conjunto finito de símbolos de entrada.  
• Λ é um conjunto finito de símbolos de saída.  
• T : S × Σ → S é a função de transição.  
• O : S × Σ → Λ é a função de saída.  

3 Associando LLMs a MEFs  
Denotamos o LLM como L(p) = t, em que p ∈ V* é um prompt e t ∈ V* é a resposta textual. Embora a entrada e a saída possam ser quaisquer sequências de tokens, apenas uma pequena fração corresponde a ações válidas.  

A MEF é derivada do PDDL do problema, projetada para receber uma ação a ∈ Σ ⊂ V* e retornar uma saída o ∈ Λ ⊂ V*, que é então adicionada ao próximo prompt p do LLM. Isso estabelece um ciclo interativo: o LLM propõe ações com base em p, enquanto a MEF modela pré-condições e efeitos. Como não há garantia de que t seja uma ação válida, definimos uma função de validação f : (V*, S) → Σ ∪ {–1} tal que  

f(tᵢ, sⱼ) =  
  { tᵢ, se tᵢ for ação válida em sⱼ  
    –1, caso contrário  

Em vez de usar t diretamente, T e O recebem f(tᵢ, sⱼ), projetando saídas inválidas para o símbolo –1.  

Para avaliar como a modelagem por MEF pode melhorar LLMs, comparamos sete métodos que variam desde um esquema de entrada/saída pré-planejado até abordagens interativas sofisticadas com validação e feedback, além de restrições. Também examinamos a técnica CoT. Nosso objetivo é investigar:  
1. É mais eficaz gerar o plano completo de uma vez ou ação a ação interagindo com a MEF?  
2. A integração de validações e ciclos de feedback melhora a eficácia em tarefas de planejamento?  
3. Que métodos restringem a gama de ações disponíveis, guiando o LLM a resultados ótimos?  

Todos os métodos utilizam o mesmo prompt de contexto p_c, com descrição da tarefa, regras (predicados e ações) e estados inicial/meta. Cada configuração tem seu próprio prompt de solicitação p_r, que pode pedir o plano inteiro ou a próxima ação. Ao início da inferência ocorre uma transição ε que envia p_c + p_r ao LLM, e o espaço de estados inclui um estado inicial artificial s_start, um s_end e os estados da tarefa s ∈ S_task.  

As três características combinadas nos métodos são:  
• Pré-planejado vs Interativo: Pré-planejado gera toda a sequência de ações de uma só vez, sem validação entre elas. Interativo gera uma ação por vez, permitindo detectar ações inválidas precocemente.  
• Sem Validação vs Validado vs Restrito:  
  – Sem validação interrompe o processo em caso de ação inválida.  
  – Validado usa f para projetar a saída e fornece feedback ao LLM se a ação for inválida.  
  – Restrito apresenta ao LLM todas as ações válidas possíveis em cada estado (numeradas), mas o modelo ainda pode gerar qualquer token; usamos uma versão modificada de f para mapear o número escolhido à ação correspondente ou –1 em caso de escolha inválida.  
• Padrão vs Chain-of-Thoughts: Padrão descreve a meta e pede o plano (ou próxima ação). CoT induz o LLM a realizar raciocínio passo a passo em cada interação.  

4 Configuração Experimental  
Usamos o domínio Block-world, que envolve manipulação de blocos identificados por cores, posicionados sobre a mesa ou empilhados uns nos outros. Cada instância define um estado inicial e um objetivo de empilhar blocos em certa ordem. As quatro ações possíveis são: pick-up, put-down, stack e unstack, com pré-condições e efeitos clássicos desse domínio. Por sua simplicidade e alinhamento com o senso comum, Block-world é amplamente adotado na literatura de planejamento.  

Geramos 768 instâncias com 4 blocos cada, balanceadas pela extensão do plano ótimo (2 a 12 ações). Usamos o mesmo prompt de contexto citado em trabalhos anteriores. Todos os prompts são zero-shot, exceto em métodos CoT, que requerem um exemplo (one-shot) para induzir raciocínio estruturado. Avaliamos três LLMs: Mixtral:8x22b, Llama3:70b e GPT-4o, todos com temperatura 0 para determinismo. Impusemos até 8 tentativas na abordagem Pré-planejado-Validado e até 16 ações inválidas nas abordagens Interativas.  

Métricas:  
– Plano Bem-Sucedido: alcança a meta sem erros.  
– Plano Válido: não contém ações inválidas.  
– Plano Ótimo: igual ao comprimento do plano ótimo.  
– Comprimento Relativo do Plano: ações geradas dividido pelo ótimo.  
– Tokens Processados (milhares).  
– Distância ao Estado Inicial e ao Estado Meta, em número mínimo de ações para alcançá-los.  

5 Resultados  
A Tabela 1 sumariza acurácia, percentuais de planos ótimos, tokens processados e comprimento relativo médio. As abordagens Interativas Validado e Restrito superam consistentemente as demais em acurácia, independentemente do modelo. CoT obteve bons resultados apenas em GPT-4o, enquanto Mixtral e Llama3 pioraram com CoT, indicando que validação por MEF oferece ganho mais consistente que prompting CoT.  

Pré-planejado alcança percentuais maiores de planos ótimos entre os poucos planos bem-sucedidos, frequentemente em tarefas simples. Métodos interativos validado tendem a produzir planos mais longos, pois interrompem a inferência assim que a MEF detecta o estado meta, mesmo que o LLM não o identifique explicitamente. Uma desvantagem dos métodos interativos é o custo computacional: eles processam cerca de dez vezes mais tokens que os pré-planejados, pois cada iteração preserva todo o histórico do prompt.  

A Tabela 2 mostra que métodos sem validação geram baixos percentuais de planos válidos, pois não lidam com alucinações do LLM. Interações validadas e restritas garantem 100% de validade, por projetarem saídas inválidas para –1 e darem feedback. Em Mixtral e Llama3, CoT gerou frequentemente ações fora do formato esperado, reforçando a sensibilidade dessas técnicas de prompting.  

Dado o desempenho superior das abordagens Interativas Validado e Restrito, focamos nelas. A Figura 4 mostra a acurácia média em função do comprimento ótimo do plano (complexidade): ambas decaem com o aumento da complexidade, mas Hover–Validated é menos sensível a tarefas mais longas, especialmente em GPT-4o. A Figura 5 (distância do estado final gerado ao estado meta) indica que, quando falham, os métodos produzem estados tão distantes quanto o inicial, não aproximando-se do objetivo. A Figura 6 (distância ao estado inicial) revela que o método Validado explora mais o espaço de estados, finalizando planos mais distantes do ponto de partida, enquanto o Restrito tende a buscas locais.  

A Figura 7 contabiliza quantas vezes cada modelo revisita estados dentro de um plano. Validado revisita menos, sugerindo exploração diversificada, ao passo que Restrito frequentemente entra em laços, repetindo estados. Esse looping parece inerente à restrição, pois o modelo tende a otimizações de curto prazo e não reconhece ciclos quando deve retornar apenas números de ação.  

6 Conclusão  
Nossos resultados mostram que incorporar MEFs como estrutura guia melhora a capacidade de LLMs em tarefas de planejamento. Ao interagir com a MEF e usar validações, ciclos de feedback e restrições, os modelos geram planos com maior acurácia em diversas complexidades. Apesar de a acurácia ainda não ser ideal, o método provê ferramenta valiosa para aprimorar inferências em raciocínio, independentemente de técnicas de prompting.  

A integração com MEFs se comparou ao CoT em configurações pré-planejadas e interativas. CoT foi eficaz apenas em GPT-4o, enquanto MEFs aumentaram a acurácia em todos os modelos, evidenciando maior consistência que engenharia de prompt. As abordagens Interativas Validado e Restrito oferecem garantia de planos válidos – avanço substancial sobre métodos tradicionais. Observamos que validação estimula exploração mais ampla do espaço de estados, beneficiando tarefas complexas, ao passo que a restrição favorece tarefas simples, mas pode levar a loops. Por fim, destacou-se a necessidade de otimizar prompts em cenários interativos, pois o custo em tokens é significativamente maior.  

Propostas futuras incluem unificar validação, feedback e restrições diretamente no processo decisório do LLM, visando torná-lo mais confiável em raciocínios de curto e longo prazo.

Improving LLMs’ Reasoning and Planning
with Finite-State Machines
Eduardo Faria Cabrera(B), Marcel Rodrigues de Barros,
and Anna Helena Reali Costa
Universidade de São Paulo, São Paulo, SP, Brazil
{eduardofcabrera,marcel.barros,anna.reali}@usp.br
Abstract. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable
capabilities across various applications but struggle with sequential
decision-making tasks like planning. This work demonstrates that inte-
grating LLMs with Finite-State Machines (FSMs) can enhance their rea-
soning and planning abilities, while also oﬀering increased reliability.
Several setup variants are compared, providing a better understanding
of how validations, feedback loops, and restrictions enhance robustness
and eﬀectiveness. A comparison to the well known Chain-of-Thoughts
approach is also provided. Our methods improve planning capabilities
of all analysed LLMs, consistently increasing the success rate in solving
tasks of varying complexities. A detailed analysis of the two best variants
are provided, highlighting their respective strengths and weaknesses.
Keywords: Large Language Models · Machine Learning · Planning ·
Graph Representations
1
Introduction
Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have surged in development, revolu-
tionizing AI capabilities. Scaling up these models has unlocked new feats, from
crafting narratives and summarizing text to coding and enhancing reasoning
skills [2,3,18]. Despite these advancements, LLMs still face challenges in basic
logical reasoning, often producing implausible claims and struggling with rudi-
mentary planning tasks [2,15]. Moreover, the opacity of their decision-making
processes poses signiﬁcant obstacles in interpreting and validating their outputs,
especially in critical domains like healthcare and ﬁnance. Thus, there is an urgent
need for methodologies to validate, guide, and interpret the decision pathways
of LLMs.
One extensively studied form of reasoning task in the AI community is plan-
ning and making sequential decisions. Planning involves executing a series of

valid actions within a deﬁned context to transition from an initial state to a goal
state [11]. Even simple planning tasks pose challenges for LLMs, as they often
struggle to achieve success rates and generate valid plans due to the require-
ment of validating each action’s feasibility in every state, backtracking previous
states and actions, and employing long-term reasoning [15]. Enhancing planning,
reasoning, and introducing guarantees in multi-step decision making problems
is crucial for improving LLMs’ reliability, which would open up their usage in
some risk averse applications.
The research community is actively developing new methods to address
multi-step problems with LLMs by enhancing their reliability, interpretability,
and robustness. One such technique is Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [19], a prompt-
based approach that incorporates intermediate reasoning steps, or “thoughts,"
alongside task input/output pairs. By decomposing the original problem into
these intermediate steps, CoT facilitates structured reasoning, thereby improv-
ing LLMs’ ability to tackle procedural problems. Empirical evidence has demon-
strated CoT’s eﬀectiveness in enhancing problem-solving capabilities [19]. Fur-
thermore, advancements have extended CoT’s capabilities, including techniques
like Self-Consistency with CoT (CoT-SC) [17] and CausalCOT [9], as well as
more complex and ﬂexible approaches like Tree-of-Thoughts [20] and Graph-of-
Thoughts [1]. However, these techniques primarily focus on reﬁning prompting
strategies without explicitly leveraging the logical structure of problems to vali-
date and guide LLMs’ reasoning processes.
Our approach associates LLMs to Finite-State Machines (FSMs), commonly
used in systems that require reliability and predictability, as a guiding struc-
ture to the decision-making processes of LLMs. This association restricts the
model’s decision at each step, providing several additional guarantees enabling
applications with tighter restrictions to beneﬁt from modern AI capabilities.
The key contributions of our work are:
Novel Approach: We introduce a novel method that incorporates FSMs as a
guiding structure for LLM decision-making processes.
Enhanced Problem-Solving: We provide evidence that validations, feedback
loops, and restrictions enabled by FSMs, derived from standard planning
language deﬁnitions, enhance LLMs’ ability to solve planning problems.
Comprehensive Comparison: We present a detailed comparison of our most
eﬀective setups, thoroughly analyzing their strengths and weaknesses in the
context of planning problems.
2
Background
This section covers essential concepts for this work. It brieﬂy explains how auto-
regressive LLMs function and their advantages in solving planning problems.
It then provides a formal deﬁnition of a planning problem. Finally, it deﬁnes a
Mealy Machine, a type of Finite-State Machine, which will be used to guide the
LLM in addressing planning problems.
112
E. F. Cabrera et al.
2.1
Large Language Models for Planning
Large language models are built upon a transformer architecture [16], which
undergoes training on a vast corpus of text samples sourced from the web.
Formally, we deﬁne a collection of examples X = (x1, x2, . . . , xN), where each
xi = (α1, α2, . . . αni) and every token αi is drawn from a predeﬁned vocab-
ulary V. Each LLM is equipped with a tokenizer responsible for converting
raw input text into a sequence of tokens, each belonging to V. LLMs typ-
ically undergo training in an auto-regressive manner, where the probability
of each token is solely dependent on its preceding tokens in the sequence,
expressed as p(xi) = ni
j=1 p(αj|α0:j−1). During training, the model parame-
ters are learned by maximizing the likelihood of the entire dataset, formulated
as p(X) = N
i=1 p(xi).
Addressing planning problems with pre-trained LLMs is highly advantageous
as these models can leverage their extensive world knowledge, commonsense
understanding, and logical reasoning abilities. The aim is to generate a sequence
of actions (a1, a2, . . . , an) to reach a desired ﬁnal state. Graph structures have
been widely used to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, with empirical
evidence showing signiﬁcant improvements in solving complex problems [13,17,
19]. The CoT approach is fundamental, modeling the inference process as a linear
chain and explicitly capturing intermediate reasoning steps. Building on CoT,
methods like Tree-of-Thoughts and Graph-of-Thoughts introduce more complex
topologies, including branches, backtracking, and aggregating reasoning steps.
Nonetheless, incorporating prompt topologies alone is insuﬃcient to tackle
planning problems. Studies such as [15] underscore the diﬃculties LLMs face
in generating valid and optimal plans. Recent research, exempliﬁed in [10,12],
suggests that integrating feedback loops can signiﬁcantly improve LLMs’ accu-
racy in planning tasks. Consequently, implementing a mechanism for validating
the model’s outputs and providing feedback emerges as a promising strategy for
enhancing its performance.
2.2
Planning Task Deﬁnition and Finite-State Machines
A planning problem can be deﬁned as a tuple P = (S, A, s0, G) [11], where:
– S is a ﬁnite set of states. Each state s ∈S is a complete assignment of values
to a set of state variables (or ﬂuents).
– s0 ∈S is the initial state.
– G ⊂S is the set of goal states where the goal condition is satisﬁed. This
condition is speciﬁed as a conjunction of literals.
– A is the set of actions, where each action a ∈A is deﬁned by its preconditions
and eﬀects:
• Preconditions pre(a) are a set of literals that must be satisﬁed for the
action to be applied.
• Eﬀects eﬀ(a) are a set of literals that describe how the state changes after
applying the action.
Improving LLMs’ Reasoning and Planning with Finite-State Machines
113
We deﬁne a transition model γ : S × A →S that describes deterministic
state transitions in the planning problem. If a state s ∈S satisﬁes pre(a), then
γ(s, a) = s′, where s′ ∈S is the new state resulting from applying eﬀ(a) to s. If
s does not satisfy pre(a), then the action cannot be applied.
The Planning Domain Deﬁnition Language (PDDL) is commonly used to
represent planning problems, allowing for the encoding of a problem by deﬁning
its domain (types of objects, predicates, and actions) and its problem instance
(initial state and goal state). There is extensive literature on planning algorithms
for various tasks. An AI planner takes a PDDL domain and problem as input and
produces a solution. Most state-of-the-art planners [6,7] are variants of heuristic-
based forward search, where PDDL encodings are used to automatically derive
a heuristic function.
Another common approach is the integration of Markov Decision Processes
(MDPs) into automated planning. MDPs are best suited for modeling stochastic
processes where maximizing rewards in uncertain contexts is crucial [4,11]. How-
ever, many mission-critical applications are modeled using deterministic ﬁnite-
state machines due to reliability and predictability requirements.
Building on this foundation, our work investigates whether simply imposing
an alphabet of interactively validated symbols can enhance LLMs’ ability to solve
planning tasks. This restriction of possible actions associated with deterministic
transitions is best encapsulated by the FSMs formalism.
A Mealy Machine is an FSM deﬁned by a 6-tuple (S, s0, Σ, Λ, T , O), where:
– S is a ﬁnite set of states.
– s0 ∈S is the initial state.
– Σ is a ﬁnite set of input alphabet.
– Λ is a ﬁnite set of output alphabet.
– T : S × Σ →S is a transition function.
– O : S × Σ →Λ is the output function.
3
Associating LLMs to FSMs
In this setup, we denote the LLM as a function L(p) = t, where a prompt p ∈V∗
is provided, and the output t ∈V∗is a text response. Note that both input and
output can be any sequence of tokens (α1, . . . , αn) ∈V∗, however, only a small
fraction of this domain constitute valid actions.
The FSM can be derived from the problem’s PDDL and is designed to receive
an action a ∈Σ ⊂V∗and return an output o ∈Λ ⊂V∗, which is appended to
the next LLM prompt p. This establishes an interactive loop between the LLM
and the FSM, where the language model proposes actions based on its context p,
while the FSM models preconditions and eﬀects. Note that in this setup there’s
no guarantee that the LLM output t is a valid action, which means the LLM
can send invalid actions (i.e. symbols) to the FSM.

However, it is possible to project t onto Σ by providing a validation function
f such that

To assess how FSM modeling can enhance the capabilities of LLMs, we eval-
uate seven distinct methods. These range from a straightforward preplanned
input/output setup to more sophisticated approaches that utilize FSMs to
receive information and provide feedback on their actions. Additionally, we exam-
ine the CoT approach, as outlined in [15], where the initial prompt induces the
model to generate structured reasoning based on a similar example.
By analysing these variations we aim to measure three key aspects:
1. Which method proves more eﬀective: generating the entire plan at once, or
generating each action individually while interacting with the FSM?
2. Does integrating validation functions and feedback loops improve LLMs’ eﬀec-
tiveness in solving planning tasks?
3. What methods can be employed to restrict the range of actions available to
LLMs, thereby guiding them towards optimal outcomes?
Initially, all methods receive the same context prompt pc sourced from [14].
This prompt includes a detailed description of the planning task, a rulebook

possible states of the task being planned.
The methods analyzed are combinations of three characteristics:
Preplanned vs Interactive: Preplanned methods involve requesting the whole
sequence of actions to the LLM before performing any kind of validation. This
setup was assessed in [15], revealing a low success rate and a high prevalence of
invalid plans. In this setup, the LLM generates the entire plan (t1, t2, . . . , tn)
solely based on pc + pr. On the other hand, interactive methods require one

4
Experimental Setup
The dataset is obtained from [14], which provides a platform to insert a valid
PDDL domain and generate instances of it. For this study, we utilized the Block-
world domain, which captures common-sense block manipulations and consists
of a set of blocks. Each block is uniquely identiﬁed by color and can be placed
either on a table or on top of other blocks. In each instance, the initial state is a
speciﬁc block arrangement, and the goal state is to arrange some of these blocks
in a stack in a particular order (Fig. 2).
The Blockworld domain includes four diﬀerent actions: pick up, put down,
stack, and unstack. The preconditions for each action are as follows:

– To put down a block, it must be on hand.
– To stack a block on another, the ﬁrst block must be on hand and the second

– To unstack a block from another, the ﬁrst block must be clear, stacked on
the second block, and the hand must be free.
This particular domain is widely adopted in the planning literature due to
its simplicity and alignment with common-sense reasoning [5,8].
In this work, we generated a dataset with 768 instances, each containing 4
blocks. The dataset is balanced in terms of optimal plan length, which ranges
from 2 to 12 actions. We use the optimal plan length as an indicator of the
instance’s complexity. For each instance, we use the same context prompt as in
[14]. All prompts are zero-shot, except for methods using a CoT approach, where
a one-shot approach is required to induce structured reasoning.
We evaluated three diﬀerent LLMs in this work: Mixtral:8x22b, Llama3:70b,
and GPT-4o. The temperature parameter is set to 0 for all models, ensuring
that each experiment is deterministic. Our goal is to verify the eﬀectiveness of
the proposed methods independently of the speciﬁc LLM used. Additionally,
a maximum of 8 tries for the Preplanned - Validated approach and 16 invalid
actions for the Interactive approaches are enforced (Fig. 3).
The following metrics are calculated for each experiment:
– Success Plan: Indicates if the generated plan successfully reaches the goal
without any errors.

Fig. 3. (Left) Interactive - Validated: We prompt the LLM to generate one action

tain any invalid actions.
– Optimal Plan: Indicates if the generated plan is the optimal plan.
– Relative Plan Length: The total number of actions in the generated plan

– Distance to Goal State: The number of actions from the ﬁnal state of the
generated plan to the goal state.
5
Results
Numerical results are presented in Table 1, displaying average values of accuracy,
optimal plan percentage, number of processed tokens and relative plan length
metrics for all methods and models. The validated and restricted interactive
methods consistently outperform other setups in most cases. They achieve higher
accuracy than their preplanned and unvalidated counterparts regardless of the
model.
An important ﬁnding is that the CoT approach achieved good results exclu-
sively with the GPT-4o model, which is speciﬁcally trained to handle CoT rea-
soning. In contrast, the Mixtral and Llama models performed worse with the
CoT scheme in both the preplanned and the interactive validated methods. This
provides evidence that FSM-based validation provides increased accuracy in a
more generic sense, being independent of how the particular LLM was trained.

A downside of using interactive methods is their increased computational

Figure 4 displays the average accuracy for each optimal plan length, serv-

length increases, accuracy decreases, indicating that planning capabilities are
sensitive to the complexity of the tasks. Furthermore, the two setups show dif-

complex tasks, particularly with GPT-4o. In contrast, the Interactive Restricted

good approximation of the goal state. However, in Fig. 6, one can see the distance
from the ﬁnal state of the produced plan to the initial state. This visualization
shows that the distances for the Interactive Validated method are greater than

This behavior is more pronounced for larger and more complex models, such as

Figure 7 presents further evidence for the diﬀerence in exploratory behavior
between the methods. It shows the average number of times each model revisited

tendency to explore diverse states. Conversely, the Interactive Restricted method
frequently revisits states, suggesting a propensity to get stuck in loops. This loop-
ing behavior is likely inherent to the restricted setup. Restricted models receive
previous actions as input, but often fail to recognize when they’re trapped in a
cycle. This potentially encourages short-term decision-making, hindering their
ability to analyze past actions and states. We suspect this issue is exacerbated
by the requirement to return action numbers instead of names in the restricted
setting. This implicit task progress representation might make it challenging for
the model to consider the entire historical trajectory when choosing the next
action. Consequently, the restricted version tends towards local optimizations,
leading to frequent loop formation.

6
Conclusion
Our results provide evidence that incorporating FSMs as a guiding structure
enhances LLMs’ ability to solve planning problems. By interacting with the
FSM and leveraging integrated validations, feedback loops, and restrictions,
LLMs demonstrably generate plans with increased accuracy across tasks of vary-
ing complexity. Although the accuracy achieved is not yet ideal, the proposed
method demonstrates a valuable tool for improving model inference in reasoning
tasks, oﬀering beneﬁts independent of other prompt engineering techniques.
FSM integration was also compared to the CoT prompting technique in both
preplanned and interactive validated schemes. CoT showed superior performance
exclusively for the GPT-4o model, while FSM integration greatly increased accu-
racy for all models. This provides evidence that FSM integration is a more consis-
tent solution than prompt engineering techniques that can behave unpredictably
across diﬀerent scenarios.
The proposed Interactive Validated and Restricted setups oﬀer a crucial
advantage by being inherently designed to handle invalid inputs, thus guar-
anteeing that all generated plans are valid. This is a substantial improvement
over traditional approaches, where LLMs frequently generate invalid plans. We
observed that incorporating validation encourages exploratory behavior in the
models, leading to better performance on complex tasks across all three com-
pared models. Conversely, while incorporating restrictions can enhance perfor-
mance on simpler tasks, it can also cause the models to enter loops, resulting in
poorer performance on more complex tasks. A signiﬁcant downside of interactive

123
approaches is their increased computational cost. Results show that the number
of tokens processed in these schemes is an order of magnitude higher than in
preplanned setups, underscoring the necessity of prompt optimization in these
scenarios.
Despite the simplicity of the experimental context, the ﬁndings open up new
avenues for future research aimed at enhancing reasoning capabilities using log-
ical structures that constrain the action space in problem-solving. The proposed
method also introduces greater predictability and robustness into the system.
Our ﬁndings suggest promising avenues for future research. One direction
involves developing approaches that can unify validation with feedback and
restrictions within the LLM’s decision-making process. This could lead to more
reliable and robust models capable of both short-term and long-term reasoning.

Melhorando o Raciocínio e o Planejamento de LLMs com Máquinas de Estados Finitos  
Eduardo Faria Cabrera(B), Marcel Rodrigues de Barros e Anna Helena Reali Costa  
Universidade de São Paulo, São Paulo, SP, Brasil  
{eduardofcabrera, marcel.barros, anna.reali}@usp.br  

Resumo. Grandes Modelos de Linguagem (LLMs) têm demonstrado capacidades notáveis em diversas aplicações, mas ainda apresentam dificuldade em tarefas de tomada de decisão sequencial, como planejamento. Este trabalho mostra que a integração de LLMs com Máquinas de Estados Finitos (FSMs) pode aprimorar suas habilidades de raciocínio e planejamento, além de oferecer maior confiabilidade. Comparamos várias configurações de uso, de forma a entender como validações, ciclos de feedback e restrições aumentam a robustez e a eficácia. Também apresentamos uma comparação com a conhecida abordagem Chain-of-Thoughts. Nossos métodos melhoram consistentemente a taxa de sucesso em resolver tarefas de diferentes níveis de complexidade para todos os LLMs analisados. Por fim, fornecemos uma análise detalhada das duas variantes mais eficazes, destacando seus pontos fortes e suas limitações.

Palavras-chave: Grandes Modelos de Linguagem · Aprendizado de Máquina · Planejamento · Representações em Grafos

1 Introdução  
Recentemente, Grandes Modelos de Linguagem (LLMs) vêm revolucionando as capacidades da IA. A ampliação desses modelos tornou possível desde a geração de narrativas e resumos até a codificação e o aprimoramento do raciocínio [2,3,18]. Ainda assim, LLMs enfrentam desafios em raciocínio lógico básico e em tarefas de planejamento, frequentemente produzindo falhas de coerência, alucinações e planos inválidos [2,15]. Além disso, a opacidade de seus processos internos dificulta a interpretação e a validação de suas saídas em domínios críticos como saúde e finanças. Por isso, há uma necessidade urgente de metodologias que orientem, validem e tornem transparente a trajetória de decisão desses modelos.

Planejamento, entendido como a execução de uma sequência de ações válidas que leva de um estado inicial a um estado meta [11], é um problema clássico de raciocínio sequencial. Mesmo tarefas de planejamento relativamente simples podem ser desafiadoras para LLMs, pois exigem a verificação de pré-condições e efeitos a cada passo, a capacidade de retroceder ações e o uso de raciocínio de longo prazo [15]. Melhorar o desempenho em planejamento é, portanto, essencial para viabilizar o uso de LLMs em cenários que requerem alta confiabilidade.

Uma das técnicas mais estudadas para tarefas multi-etapa é o Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [19], que inclui nos prompts passos intermediários de raciocínio (“pensamentos”) para guiar a geração de respostas. Extensões como Self-Consistency with CoT (CoT-SC) [17], CausalCOT [9], Tree-of-Thoughts [20] e Graph-of-Thoughts [1] exploram topologias mais complexas, mas não se aproveitam explicitamente da estrutura lógica do problema para validar as decisões geradas pelo LLM.

Neste trabalho, propomos usar Máquinas de Estados Finitos (FSMs) como uma estrutura de orientação para as decisões do LLM. As FSMs são formalismos amplamente conhecidos em sistemas que exigem previsibilidade e confiabilidade. Ao interagir passo a passo com a FSM, o LLM tem seu espaço de ações restrito a símbolos validados, recebe feedback imediato sobre a validade de cada ação e é guiado por regras determinísticas extraídas da definição PDDL do problema.

Contribuições principais:  
• Abordagem nova: introduzimos a integração de FSMs como estrutura de orientação para a inferência de LLMs.  
• Melhora no desempenho: mostramos que validações, ciclos de feedback e restrições fornecidos pela FSM melhoram a eficácia dos LLMs em tarefas de planejamento.  
• Comparação abrangente: apresentamos um estudo detalhado de sete configurações combinando geração pré-planejada ou interativa, com ou sem validação/restrição, e com prompting padrão ou CoT.

2 Fundamentos  
2.1 Grandes Modelos de Linguagem para Planejamento  
LLMs baseiam-se na arquitetura *transformer* [16] e são treinados autorregressivamente em enormes corpora de texto. Formalmente, dados exemplos X = (x₁, …, x_N) e vocabulário V, cada sequência xi = (α₁, …, αₙᵢ) tem probabilidade  
p(xᵢ) = ∏_{j=1}^{nᵢ} p(αⱼ | α₀:ⱼ₋₁).  
Durante a inferência, a meta é gerar uma sequência de ações (a₁, …, aₙ) que leva de um estado inicial a um estado meta. Abordagens como Chain-of-Thought modelam esse processo como uma cadeia de raciocínio, mas não garantem a validade das ações geradas.

2.2 Definição de Planejamento e Máquinas de Estados Finitos  
Um problema de planejamento é a tupla P = (S, A, s₀, G) [11], onde:  
• S: conjunto de estados.  
• s₀ ∈ S: estado inicial.  
• G ⊂ S: estados meta (condição de meta como conjunção de literais).  
• A: conjunto de ações, cada a ∈ A com pré-condições pre(a) e efeitos eff(a).  
A transição determinística γ: S×A→S aplica a ação a em s se pre(a) ⊆ s, produzindo γ(s,a)=s′. Em PDDL define-se o domínio (tipos, predicados, ações) e o problema (s₀,e G). Muitos planejadores [6,7] usam busca heurística para frente; MDPs oferecem modelagem estocástica [4,11], mas sistemas críticos geralmente empregam FSMs determinísticas.

Uma Máquina de Mealy é a 6-tupla (S, s₀, Σ, Λ, T, O), onde Σ é o alfabeto de entradas (ações), Λ o alfabeto de saídas (feedback), T: S×Σ→S a função de transição e O: S×Σ→Λ a função de saída.

3 Integração de LLMs e FSMs  
Denotamos o LLM por L(p)=t, com p∈V* e t∈V*. A FSM recebe símbolos a∈Σ⊂V* e retorna feedback o∈Λ, que é concatenado ao próximo prompt. Para garantir que t seja um símbolo válido em Σ (ou sinalizar erro), definimos f:(V*,S)→Σ∪{−1}, onde  
f(tᵢ,sⱼ) = tᵢ, se tᵢ∈Σ válido em sⱼ; −1, caso contrário.  
As transições e saídas da FSM então usam f(tᵢ,sⱼ) em T(sⱼ,·) e O(sⱼ,·).

Testamos sete métodos, combinando:  
• Geração pré-planejada (plano completo de uma vez) vs geração interativa (uma ação por vez em loop com a FSM).  
• Sem validação vs Validado (feedback de ação inválida) vs Restrito (apresenta ao LLM lista numerada de ações válidas em cada estado).  
• Prompting padrão vs Chain-of-Thought (CoT).

Em todos os casos usamos o mesmo prompt de contexto pc (descrição da tarefa, regras e estados inicial/meta) e um prompt de requisição pr específico para cada método. A inferência inicia com transição ε da FSM, produzindo pc+pr como primeiro prompt. O espaço de estados é {s_start, s_end}∪S_tarefa.

4 Configuração Experimental  
Escolhemos o domínio Blockworld (manipulação de blocos), instanciado em 768 problemas com 4 blocos cada. O comprimento ótimo de plano varia de 2 a 12 ações e serve de métrica de complexidade. Para cada instância usamos zero-shot, exceto em métodos CoT (one-shot).

Modelos avaliados: Mixtral:8x22b, Llama3:70b e GPT-4o, todos com *temperature*=0. Limites: até 8 tentativas para Pré-planejado-Validado; até 16 ações inválidas nos métodos interativos.

Métricas:  
• Sucesso do plano (atingiu G sem erros)  
• Plano válido (sem ações inválidas)  
• Plano ótimo  
• Comprimento relativo (|plano|/|planoₒₚₜᵢₘₒ|)  
• Tokens processados (milhares)  
• Distância ao estado inicial/meta para planos não bem-sucedidos

5 Resultados  
A Tabela 1 mostra que os métodos interativos validados e restritos superam os demais em acurácia, independentemente do modelo. CoT foi vantajoso apenas no GPT-4o; Mixtral e Llama3 pioraram com CoT, evidenciando que a validação via FSM é mais robusta que engenharia de prompt.  

Pré-planejados tendem a ter maior percentual de planos ótimos (pois geram menos soluções e, em geral, para tarefas mais simples). Métodos interativos validados produzem planos mais longos — interrompem a inferência ao alcançar G de modo determinístico, evitando depender do LLM para reconhecer estado meta.

Um ponto fraco dos métodos interativos é o custo computacional: eles processam cerca de 10× mais tokens que os pré-planejados, pois cada iteração inclui todo o histórico de prompts. CoT também aumenta significativamente o número de tokens.

A Tabela 2 confirma que os métodos sem validação geram muitos planos inválidos. Os métodos interativos validados e restritos, por construção, garantem planos válidos, pois tratam cada entrada inválida do LLM.

Focamos então nas variantes Interativo-Validado e Interativo-Restrito. A Figura 4 mostra que a acurácia média decresce com o comprimento ótimo do plano; o método validado é menos sensível à complexidade do que o restrito. As Figuras 5 e 6 analisam, para planos que não alcançam G, a distância do estado final a G e a s₀, respectivamente. Observa-se que ambos ficam, em média, tão distantes da meta quanto do estado inicial, mas o método validado explora mais o espaço de estados (distância maior a s₀) enquanto o restrito tende a buscas locais (distância menor a s₀). A Figura 7 revela que o validado revisita menos estados (maior exploração), ao passo que o restrito frequentemente entra em ciclos, revisitando estados — comportamento possivelmente agravado pelo uso de índices numéricos de ações, que dificulta ao LLM saber que está “preso” em um loop.

6 Conclusão  
Demonstramos que a integração de FSMs como estrutura de orientação melhora significativamente o desempenho de LLMs em tarefas de planejamento, ao passo que técnicas de prompting (CoT) se mostram menos consistentes. Métodos interativos validados e restritos garantem planos válidos e aumentam a robustez, embora demandem mais tokens. A validação estimula exploração mais ampla, beneficiando problemas complexos, enquanto a restrição favorece tarefas simples, mas pode levar a loops em cenários mais difíceis.

Esses resultados abrem novas fronteiras para pesquisas que unam validação, feedback e restrição estrutural ao processo decisório de LLMs, em busca de modelos de raciocínio mais confiáveis e interpretáveis, capazes de dominar tanto o raciocínio local quanto o de longo prazo.

Improving LLMs’ Reasoning and Planning
with Finite-State Machines
Eduardo Faria Cabrera(B), Marcel Rodrigues de Barros,
and Anna Helena Reali Costa
Universidade de São Paulo, São Paulo, SP, Brazil
{eduardofcabrera,marcel.barros,anna.reali}@usp.br
Abstract. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable
capabilities across various applications but struggle with sequential
decision-making tasks like planning. This work demonstrates that inte-
grating LLMs with Finite-State Machines (FSMs) can enhance their rea-
soning and planning abilities, while also oﬀering increased reliability.
Several setup variants are compared, providing a better understanding
of how validations, feedback loops, and restrictions enhance robustness
and eﬀectiveness. A comparison to the well known Chain-of-Thoughts
approach is also provided. Our methods improve planning capabilities
of all analysed LLMs, consistently increasing the success rate in solving
tasks of varying complexities. A detailed analysis of the two best variants
are provided, highlighting their respective strengths and weaknesses.
Keywords: Large Language Models · Machine Learning · Planning ·
Graph Representations
1
Introduction
Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have surged in development, revolu-
tionizing AI capabilities. Scaling up these models has unlocked new feats, from
crafting narratives and summarizing text to coding and enhancing reasoning
skills [2,3,18]. Despite these advancements, LLMs still face challenges in basic
logical reasoning, often producing implausible claims and struggling with rudi-
mentary planning tasks [2,15]. Moreover, the opacity of their decision-making
processes poses signiﬁcant obstacles in interpreting and validating their outputs,
especially in critical domains like healthcare and ﬁnance. Thus, there is an urgent
need for methodologies to validate, guide, and interpret the decision pathways
of LLMs.
One extensively studied form of reasoning task in the AI community is plan-
ning and making sequential decisions. Planning involves executing a series of

Improving LLMs’ Reasoning and Planning with Finite-State Machines
111
valid actions within a deﬁned context to transition from an initial state to a goal
state [11]. Even simple planning tasks pose challenges for LLMs, as they often
struggle to achieve success rates and generate valid plans due to the require-
ment of validating each action’s feasibility in every state, backtracking previous
states and actions, and employing long-term reasoning [15]. Enhancing planning,
reasoning, and introducing guarantees in multi-step decision making problems
is crucial for improving LLMs’ reliability, which would open up their usage in
some risk averse applications.
The research community is actively developing new methods to address
multi-step problems with LLMs by enhancing their reliability, interpretability,
and robustness. One such technique is Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [19], a prompt-
based approach that incorporates intermediate reasoning steps, or “thoughts,"
alongside task input/output pairs. By decomposing the original problem into
these intermediate steps, CoT facilitates structured reasoning, thereby improv-
ing LLMs’ ability to tackle procedural problems. Empirical evidence has demon-
strated CoT’s eﬀectiveness in enhancing problem-solving capabilities [19]. Fur-
thermore, advancements have extended CoT’s capabilities, including techniques
like Self-Consistency with CoT (CoT-SC) [17] and CausalCOT [9], as well as
more complex and ﬂexible approaches like Tree-of-Thoughts [20] and Graph-of-
Thoughts [1]. However, these techniques primarily focus on reﬁning prompting
strategies without explicitly leveraging the logical structure of problems to vali-
date and guide LLMs’ reasoning processes.
Our approach associates LLMs to Finite-State Machines (FSMs), commonly
used in systems that require reliability and predictability, as a guiding struc-
ture to the decision-making processes of LLMs. This association restricts the
model’s decision at each step, providing several additional guarantees enabling
applications with tighter restrictions to beneﬁt from modern AI capabilities.
The key contributions of our work are:
Novel Approach: We introduce a novel method that incorporates FSMs as a
guiding structure for LLM decision-making processes.
Enhanced Problem-Solving: We provide evidence that validations, feedback
loops, and restrictions enabled by FSMs, derived from standard planning
language deﬁnitions, enhance LLMs’ ability to solve planning problems.
Comprehensive Comparison: We present a detailed comparison of our most
eﬀective setups, thoroughly analyzing their strengths and weaknesses in the
context of planning problems.
2
Background
This section covers essential concepts for this work. It brieﬂy explains how auto-
regressive LLMs function and their advantages in solving planning problems.
It then provides a formal deﬁnition of a planning problem. Finally, it deﬁnes a
Mealy Machine, a type of Finite-State Machine, which will be used to guide the
LLM in addressing planning problems.
112
E. F. Cabrera et al.
2.1
Large Language Models for Planning
Large language models are built upon a transformer architecture [16], which
undergoes training on a vast corpus of text samples sourced from the web.
Formally, we deﬁne a collection of examples X = (x1, x2, . . . , xN), where each
xi = (α1, α2, . . . αni) and every token αi is drawn from a predeﬁned vocab-
ulary V. Each LLM is equipped with a tokenizer responsible for converting
raw input text into a sequence of tokens, each belonging to V. LLMs typ-
ically undergo training in an auto-regressive manner, where the probability
of each token is solely dependent on its preceding tokens in the sequence,
expressed as p(xi) = ni
j=1 p(αj|α0:j−1). During training, the model parame-
ters are learned by maximizing the likelihood of the entire dataset, formulated
as p(X) = N
i=1 p(xi).
Addressing planning problems with pre-trained LLMs is highly advantageous
as these models can leverage their extensive world knowledge, commonsense
understanding, and logical reasoning abilities. The aim is to generate a sequence
of actions (a1, a2, . . . , an) to reach a desired ﬁnal state. Graph structures have
been widely used to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, with empirical
evidence showing signiﬁcant improvements in solving complex problems [13,17,
19]. The CoT approach is fundamental, modeling the inference process as a linear
chain and explicitly capturing intermediate reasoning steps. Building on CoT,
methods like Tree-of-Thoughts and Graph-of-Thoughts introduce more complex
topologies, including branches, backtracking, and aggregating reasoning steps.
Nonetheless, incorporating prompt topologies alone is insuﬃcient to tackle
planning problems. Studies such as [15] underscore the diﬃculties LLMs face
in generating valid and optimal plans. Recent research, exempliﬁed in [10,12],
suggests that integrating feedback loops can signiﬁcantly improve LLMs’ accu-
racy in planning tasks. Consequently, implementing a mechanism for validating
the model’s outputs and providing feedback emerges as a promising strategy for
enhancing its performance.
2.2
Planning Task Deﬁnition and Finite-State Machines
A planning problem can be deﬁned as a tuple P = (S, A, s0, G) [11], where:
– S is a ﬁnite set of states. Each state s ∈S is a complete assignment of values
to a set of state variables (or ﬂuents).
– s0 ∈S is the initial state.
– G ⊂S is the set of goal states where the goal condition is satisﬁed. This
condition is speciﬁed as a conjunction of literals.
– A is the set of actions, where each action a ∈A is deﬁned by its preconditions
and eﬀects:
• Preconditions pre(a) are a set of literals that must be satisﬁed for the
action to be applied.
• Eﬀects eﬀ(a) are a set of literals that describe how the state changes after
applying the action.
Improving LLMs’ Reasoning and Planning with Finite-State Machines
113
We deﬁne a transition model γ : S × A →S that describes deterministic
state transitions in the planning problem. If a state s ∈S satisﬁes pre(a), then
γ(s, a) = s′, where s′ ∈S is the new state resulting from applying eﬀ(a) to s. If
s does not satisfy pre(a), then the action cannot be applied.
The Planning Domain Deﬁnition Language (PDDL) is commonly used to
represent planning problems, allowing for the encoding of a problem by deﬁning
its domain (types of objects, predicates, and actions) and its problem instance
(initial state and goal state). There is extensive literature on planning algorithms
for various tasks. An AI planner takes a PDDL domain and problem as input and
produces a solution. Most state-of-the-art planners [6,7] are variants of heuristic-
based forward search, where PDDL encodings are used to automatically derive
a heuristic function.
Another common approach is the integration of Markov Decision Processes
(MDPs) into automated planning. MDPs are best suited for modeling stochastic
processes where maximizing rewards in uncertain contexts is crucial [4,11]. How-
ever, many mission-critical applications are modeled using deterministic ﬁnite-
state machines due to reliability and predictability requirements.
Building on this foundation, our work investigates whether simply imposing
an alphabet of interactively validated symbols can enhance LLMs’ ability to solve
planning tasks. This restriction of possible actions associated with deterministic
transitions is best encapsulated by the FSMs formalism.
A Mealy Machine is an FSM deﬁned by a 6-tuple (S, s0, Σ, Λ, T , O), where:
– S is a ﬁnite set of states.
– s0 ∈S is the initial state.
– Σ is a ﬁnite set of input alphabet.
– Λ is a ﬁnite set of output alphabet.
– T : S × Σ →S is a transition function.
– O : S × Σ →Λ is the output function.
3
Associating LLMs to FSMs
In this setup, we denote the LLM as a function L(p) = t, where a prompt p ∈V∗
is provided, and the output t ∈V∗is a text response. Note that both input and
output can be any sequence of tokens (α1, . . . , αn) ∈V∗, however, only a small
fraction of this domain constitute valid actions.
The FSM can be derived from the problem’s PDDL and is designed to receive
an action a ∈Σ ⊂V∗and return an output o ∈Λ ⊂V∗, which is appended to
the next LLM prompt p. This establishes an interactive loop between the LLM
and the FSM, where the language model proposes actions based on its context p,
while the FSM models preconditions and eﬀects. Note that in this setup there’s
no guarantee that the LLM output t is a valid action, which means the LLM
can send invalid actions (i.e. symbols) to the FSM.

f such that

This function checks whether t corresponds to a valid action for the current
state, producing a common symbol −1 for invalid actions. Consequently, instead
of the FSM’s transition and output functions receiving t, they use the output
from the validation function: T (sj, f(ti, sj)) and O(sj, f(ti, sj)).
To assess how FSM modeling can enhance the capabilities of LLMs, we eval-
uate seven distinct methods. These range from a straightforward preplanned
input/output setup to more sophisticated approaches that utilize FSMs to
receive information and provide feedback on their actions. Additionally, we exam-
ine the CoT approach, as outlined in [15], where the initial prompt induces the
model to generate structured reasoning based on a similar example.
By analysing these variations we aim to measure three key aspects:
1. Which method proves more eﬀective: generating the entire plan at once, or
generating each action individually while interacting with the FSM?
2. Does integrating validation functions and feedback loops improve LLMs’ eﬀec-
tiveness in solving planning tasks?
3. What methods can be employed to restrict the range of actions available to
LLMs, thereby guiding them towards optimal outcomes?
Initially, all methods receive the same context prompt pc sourced from [14].
This prompt includes a detailed description of the planning task, a rulebook
outlining all predicates and actions, and information about the current and goal
states, as shown in Fig. 1. Each setup has its own request prompt pr, which
solicits either the entire plan or individual actions, enabling customization based
on each setup’s speciﬁc approach.
When the inference begins, the epsilon-transition T (sstart, ϵ) = s0 occurs and
the respective output O(sstart, ϵ) = pc + pr produces the initial prompt. Thus,
the state space becomes S = {sstart, send} ∪Stask, where Stask is the set of all
possible states of the task being planned.
The methods analyzed are combinations of three characteristics:
Preplanned vs Interactive: Preplanned methods involve requesting the whole
sequence of actions to the LLM before performing any kind of validation. This
setup was assessed in [15], revealing a low success rate and a high prevalence of
invalid plans. In this setup, the LLM generates the entire plan (t1, t2, . . . , tn)
solely based on pc + pr. On the other hand, interactive methods require one
action at a time, performing an interaction between FSM and LLM at each
step, allowing for invalid actions to be recognized earlier, preventing a reset
back to s0.

115
No Validation vs Validated vs Restricted: Three diﬀerent schemes of vali-

validation scheme simply halts the process in the case of invalid plans or
actions. The validated scheme makes use of f to guarantee LLM outputs are
projected onto Σ and provides feedback in the case of invalid actions. Finally,
restricted methods provide all valid actions (obtained from the PDDL) for a
certain state to the LLM through O. In this case the LLM is asked to choose
the number ti corresponding to the selected action, but can still output any

4
Experimental Setup
The dataset is obtained from [14], which provides a platform to insert a valid
PDDL domain and generate instances of it. For this study, we utilized the Block-
world domain, which captures common-sense block manipulations and consists
of a set of blocks. Each block is uniquely identiﬁed by color and can be placed
either on a table or on top of other blocks. In each instance, the initial state is a
speciﬁc block arrangement, and the goal state is to arrange some of these blocks
in a stack in a particular order (Fig. 2).
The Blockworld domain includes four diﬀerent actions: pick up, put down,
stack, and unstack. The preconditions for each action are as follows:
116
E. F. Cabrera et al.
Fig. 2. (Left) Preplanned - Validated: We prompt the LLM to generate the entire
plan in a single step. If the plan is invalid, we provide feedback and prompt the LLM
to generate a new plan. (Right) Interactive - No Validation: We prompt the LLM
to generate one action at a time and check if the goal is reached after each action.
This process continues until the LLM indicates that the goal has been reached or the
maximum number of iterations is exceeded.
– To pick up a block, it must be clear (no block stacked on it), on the table,
and the hand must be free.
– To put down a block, it must be on hand.
– To stack a block on another, the ﬁrst block must be on hand and the second
block must be clear.
– To unstack a block from another, the ﬁrst block must be clear, stacked on
the second block, and the hand must be free.
This particular domain is widely adopted in the planning literature due to
its simplicity and alignment with common-sense reasoning [5,8].
In this work, we generated a dataset with 768 instances, each containing 4
blocks. The dataset is balanced in terms of optimal plan length, which ranges
from 2 to 12 actions. We use the optimal plan length as an indicator of the
instance’s complexity. For each instance, we use the same context prompt as in
[14]. All prompts are zero-shot, except for methods using a CoT approach, where
a one-shot approach is required to induce structured reasoning.
We evaluated three diﬀerent LLMs in this work: Mixtral:8x22b, Llama3:70b,
and GPT-4o. The temperature parameter is set to 0 for all models, ensuring
that each experiment is deterministic. Our goal is to verify the eﬀectiveness of
the proposed methods independently of the speciﬁc LLM used. Additionally,
a maximum of 8 tries for the Preplanned - Validated approach and 16 invalid
actions for the Interactive approaches are enforced (Fig. 3).
The following metrics are calculated for each experiment:
– Success Plan: Indicates if the generated plan successfully reaches the goal
without any errors.
